title: El Niño Has Destroyed 85 Percent of India's Alphonso Mango Crop. The Iran War Took Care of the Rest.
excerpt: Maharashtra's 'King of Mangoes' has suffered its worst season in decades. Farmers in Devgad are scrambling to survive, exports have collapsed, and the diaspora's favorite summer fruit is vanishing from shelves abroad.
body:
In the coastal town of Devgad, Maharashtra's mango heartland, Komal Walke's three acres of orchards produced almost nothing this year.

The 26-year-old horticulturist has been forced to source Alphonso mangoes from larger farms to fulfill orders from India's online grocers — a desperate measure to keep her father's business alive. "If we don't deliver on our orders, the big clients will not return next year," she told Reuters.

Walke is not alone. A government-backed survey by scientists and field officials estimates this year's Alphonso crop losses in Devgad at 85 to 90 percent. Across Maharashtra, production is among the lowest in decades.

## What Happened

The damage came in two waves. First, a sharp difference between daytime and nighttime temperatures in December and January disrupted flowering and fruit setting — the critical early stage of mango development. Then, hotter-than-usual weather in April and May, driven by the emerging El Niño pattern, spoiled the fruits themselves.

El Niño, a climate pattern that warms Pacific Ocean surface temperatures, is expected to strengthen through 2026. India's Meteorological Department has already forecast a below-normal monsoon — the first such prediction in eight years — raising concerns that the damage to agriculture will extend well beyond mangoes.

India is the world's largest mango producer, growing 28 million metric tons in 2024-25. The entire mango market was worth $2.3 billion last year, according to research firm Mordor Intelligence, with $56 million in fresh mango exports and $80 million in mango pulp exports.

## The War Killed Exports

Even without El Niño, this would have been a brutal year for mango exporters. The Iran war has disrupted shipping routes through the Strait of Hormuz, doubling freight charges and causing delays or outright cancellations of consignments to the Gulf.

The UAE, Kuwait, Qatar, the U.S., and the UK are India's biggest mango importers. Shridhar Pathak, co-founder of mango exporter Shreevali Agro, told Reuters that his shipments to Dubai and Oman have dropped nearly 40 percent this year.

Mangoes originally earmarked for export have been dumped on domestic markets instead, creating a paradox: despite catastrophic crop losses, local prices have actually fallen because export-grade fruit is flooding bazaars.

## The Diaspora Feels It

For NRIs, the Alphonso mango is more than a fruit — it is a seasonal ritual. Every summer, Indian grocery stores in New Jersey, London, Toronto, and Dubai stock cases of Alphonso mangoes, often pre-ordered weeks in advance. This year, supply is cratering.

Indian grocery stores in the U.S. and UK are reporting sharply reduced shipments of Alphonso mangoes, with some retailers unable to fill pre-orders at all. Prices for the boxes that do arrive have jumped 40 to 60 percent compared to last year.

The ripple effects extend across the supply chain. Sanjay Nare, a 52-year-old manufacturer of mango cartons in the coastal town of Malvan — about 50 kilometers from Devgad — has nearly 100,000 unsold boxes sitting in his factory. "The economy in this region is sustained by mangoes and fishes," he said. "Without our seasonal mangoes, we have very little else."

## What's Next

The El Niño forecast suggests 2026 could be a bad year for Indian agriculture broadly. The IMD's below-normal monsoon prediction has already prompted states like Odisha to roll out emergency Kharif preparedness plans, including short-duration crop varieties, buffer seed stocks, and expanded crop insurance enrollment.

For Alphonso mango farmers, the damage is already done. Recovery depends on two things: whether the monsoon brings enough rain to replenish orchards, and whether shipping routes normalize by next season. Neither is guaranteed.

India's $2.3 billion mango industry — and the millions of farmers, traders, box makers, and exporters who depend on it — is learning what happens when climate and geopolitics hit at the same time.
author: Diaspora Desk
